transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Early voting this year outpaced numbers from the last midterm elections in 2022.
As NPR's Hansi Luang reports, more than 49 million ballots have already been cast, less
than three days until Election Day.
Around the country, voters have returned more than 22 million mail-in ballots as of Friday.
They've also cast more than 26 million ballots in person at early voting sites.
That's according to statistics compiled by the University of Florida's Election Lab.
And altogether, that's higher than the total early voting numbers for the 2022 midterms.
This year's numbers are expected to taper off, as some states end early in-person voting
before Election Day.
For mail-in voters who haven't returned their ballots yet, it is likely too late now for
the U.S. Postal Service to deliver them in time for them to be received by Election Day.
Voters can consider returning their mail-in ballot at their local election office or at
any available ballot drop box instead.
Hansi Luang, NPR News.
The federal judge is opening an inquiry into potential misconduct by Trump administration
officials in carrying out President Trump's plans to renovate a historic public golf course
in Washington, D.C.
And here's Rachel Triesman has more.
Justice department lawyers have repeatedly contradicted President Trump's social media
posts by telling district judge Ana Reyes that there is no imminent plan to close East
Potomac for renovations in mid-November.
They changed course in court filings this week, prompting Reyes to order this latest hearing.
Reyes grilled the government's lawyers about details of the plan, which they now say will
keep much of the riverfront park closed to repair its deteriorating seawall.
Reyes closed the four-hour hearing by announcing an inquiry into officials' conduct in the
case, including whether they misrepresented the government's plans for the municipal golf
course.
She says she will select a special master to lead that investigation, or if the government
prefers, conduct it herself.
Rachel Triesman, NPR News.
California's Governor Gavin Newsom has until Monday to decide whether the state takes the
$1.42 billion in federal broadband money to connect homes and businesses without good
internet service.
This is Rachel Myro of Member Station KQED reports, the funding comes with a catch.
A Trump administration provision attached to the funds would bar the state from enforcing
many of its own consumer protection rules for about 14 years, including a ban on slowing
firefighters' data during emergencies.
California is the last holdout, and Regina Costa of the consumer group Tern, the utility
reform network, says it should stay that way.
And it's a bad trade-off because California is being asked to sign all of its rights away
in exchange for a pot of money that pales in comparison to what we already have.
AT&T, Comcast and Verizon, among the companies in line for the money, did not respond to
requests for comment.
For NPR News, I'm Rachel Myro.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
For the third weekend in a row, protesters are out in force in France, angry over the
rising cost of living and education.
Tens of thousands of police have been deployed around the country, and France's interior
minister says there's a risk of problems, especially after dark, on this Halloween.
The protests started last month with high school students and have grown to include
labor unions and others.
Similar youth-led protests have taken place in Germany and Italy over education, health,
the economy, and climate protection.
Tomorrow marks the end of daylight saving time.
Many Americans will turn their clocks back one hour.
And here's Ava Berger reports, the future of the over-a-century-long practice is uncertain.
An extra hour of sleep is just a day away.
At 2 a.m. Sunday morning, many clocks across the country will be sent backwards one hour.
This twice-yearly change has once again become political.
According to a Gallup poll from last year, more than half of Americans want daylight
saving time gone.
President Donald Trump agrees.
He wants to make daylight saving time permanent.
That means the clocks won't change.
Here's what he told auto workers during a July speech in Michigan.
Let's get rid of daylight saving time stuff, OK?
A bipartisan bill to do just that, the Sunshine Protection Act, is stuck in the Senate.
So tomorrow, the clocks will still jump back.
Ava Berger, NPR News.
On Wall Street this week, all of the major market indices ended the week in red.
The Dow fell more than eight-tenths of a percent.
The NASDAQ, the tech-heavy NASDAQ, dropped two percent.
You're listening to NPR.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
Plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: Early voting this year surpasses 2022 midterm totals, with over 49 million ballots cast
Federal judge Ana Reyes opens inquiry into Trump administration conduct over East Potomac golf course renovation
California's Governor Newsom weighs $1.42 billion federal broadband funding with consumer protection rollback provision
Protests across France over cost of living and education enter third weekend, with tens of thousands of police deployed
Americans prepare to turn clocks back for end of daylight saving time, as permanent-time bill stalls in Senate
Wall Street ends the week lower, with the Dow down more than 0.8% and NASDAQ down 2%
